keep: Her union trademarked her slogan. A president told her he had stolen it.
lede: She co-founded the farm workers' union and spent her career at the bargaining table and in the statehouse. The line everyone chants was her answer to a room that said it could not be done.
copy: She was born in Dawson, New Mexico, in 1930 and grew up in Stockton, California, where she earned a provisional teaching credential. By her foundation's account she left the classroom because she could no longer bear to see her students come to school hungry and barefoot. She met Cesar Chavez through the Community Service Organization in 1955, and in the spring of 1962 the two of them resigned from it and launched the National Farm Workers Association, which became the United Farm Workers. Her work was the part that does not photograph. In 1963 she won state aid for dependent families and disability insurance for California farm workers. She helped lead the grape boycott that forced growers into some of the country's first farm worker contracts. She was instrumental in the Agricultural Labor Relations Act of 1975, which her foundation calls the first law of its kind in the country: it gave California's farm workers the right to organise and bargain.

In May 1972 Chavez was fasting in Phoenix against a grower-backed Arizona law that made it all but impossible for farm workers to organise. Local Latino labour and political leaders came to brief the two of them and kept saying the industry was too strong: no se puede. Huerta answered: sí, se puede. That is the union's own account, and the union has since registered the phrase as a trademark. In 2012 a president who had run on it in English gave her the Presidential Medal of Freedom and said at the ceremony that he had told her he had stolen her slogan.

On 14 September 1988, aged fifty-eight, she was protesting in San Francisco against the policies of George Bush, then running for president. A police officer clubbed her with a baton. The spleen had to be removed. In 1991 the city paid her $825,000, and the department changed its rules on crowd control and police discipline. She took a leave from the union after a long recovery, spent two years on the road for the Feminist Majority, and went back to organising.

facts.s: Paid to her in 1991 after the 1988 clubbing: 'S.F.'s legal costs', San Francisco Examiner, 4 March 1997 (sfgate.com), a list of the city's police settlements
Her age at the 14 September 1988 assault: Dolores Huerta Foundation, 'Dolores Huerta' (doloreshuerta.org/dolores-huerta)
Ribs broken in the assault: La Voz de Aztlán, 19 September 1988 (Fresno State Library, omeka.library.fresnostate.edu/s/la-voz/item/1183), says two; the Dolores Huerta Foundation says four
Her children: Barack Obama, remarks at the Presidential Medal of Freedom ceremony, 29 May 2012 (obamawhitehouse.archives.gov), says seven; the Dolores Huerta Foundation says eleven

bio.why: Her own speeches, interviews and writing, which is the way round it has to be for someone whose problem is that other people have narrated her. Biographies of Chavez cover the same decades and are far easier to find. Start here, not there.

contested: The record does not agree on its own numbers, and the disagreements run in one direction. La Voz de Aztlán, a Fresno State paper, reported five days after the beating that she had two broken ribs; her foundation now says four. Obama, at the 2012 ceremony, called her a single mother of seven; the foundation counts eleven children. The slogan's credit rests on the union's account and her foundation's, which the National Archives' history office repeats, and none of them is a disinterested witness. The larger argument, over how the credit for the farm workers' movement should be divided between her and Chavez and where she stood against him, belongs to the union's historians. This entry has not opened their books and does not take a side in it.

across.label: Martin Luther King Jr.
across.txt: — the same decade and the same problem: a movement gets one remembered face, and the organisers behind it are the ones who made it work.
